newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's anti-communists look set to govern.
newsitem.headline: Romania's anti-communists look set to govern.

text.p: The race for Romania's presidency remained open on Monday but the country looked set for a political sea change as election exit polls suggested the anti-communist opposition would have its first chance to govern.

Exit polls broadcast on Romanian television put the Democratic Convention (CDR), a grouping of 15 parties, in the lead in Sunday's parliamentary polls and dealt a rebuff to President Ion Iliescu's ruling left-wingers.

Up to 1,000 CDR supporters tooted car horns through central Bucharest and converged on University Square, the capital's traditional site for demonstrations, waving portraits of the Convention's leader, professor Emil Constantinescu.
"There are four years of hard work ahead of us," the bearded Constantinescu told the mainly young crowd from atop a parked car long after midnight. "Together we will succeed."

The CDR scored between 32 and 35 percent of the vote in the exit polls to 22-25 percent for Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), which the opposition blames for timid reforms and economic decline. The PDSR has run Romania, in one form or another, since the 1989 collapse of communism.

Results were due to start trickling in on Monday afternoon. If confirmed, the exit polls score should be sufficient to enable the Convention to govern in coalition with other parties clearing the minimum three percent barrier to enter parliament.

Exit polls for the presidential race were split, one sponsored by state television putting Iliescu three points ahead and two others by private channels giving Constantinescu a thin edge. The two men are nearly certain to meet in a November 17 run-off.
Commentators noted the outcome would amount to the first time since 1928 that Romania had undergone a peaceful transition of government through the ballot box.

"The election will be a big shock to Romanians," political analyst Bogdan Teodorescu told Reuters. "We will learn that there can be change without anyone being killed. People no longer in power don't go to jail. Their heads are not cut off."

The Convention based its campaign on a "Contract with Romanians" pledging to resign within 200 days if it fails to speed up reforms and tackle the mass poverty that has engulfed millions in the post-communist era.

The CDR has ruled out a coalition with Iliescu's PDSR. Its natural allies could be the third-place Social Democrats (USD) of former prime minister Petre Roman, who also ended third in the presidential stakes.

Iliescu's performance was little short of disastrous. A poor showing had been expected by his scandal-ridden party in the parliamentary poll but he had hoped to use his popularity in the countryside to finish clear of the presidential field.
Activists of his PDSR said a slight drop in support was acceptable given the misery of the transition to the market economy. But Iliescu's chances do not appear bright in the run-off.

"Anything is possible. Negotiations are open for any types of possible alternative," a dejected Iliescu told reporters. He hinted an alliance linking his PDSR to the Convention might be more stable than one grouping the two opposition parties.
Election turnout was just over 70 percent, a high figure that had been thought to favour Iliescu.
Iliescu portrayed his opponents as risk-takers and himself as a guarantor of stability.
